$comment: Whatever is under apps/ is on the test mirror a moment later, without anyone asking for it.
The rule was already written down - tests/run.sh refreshes the mirror first thing - and it held
only for as long as the battery was actually run after an edit. It was not: a UI change verified
with the render probe alone left the folder Chrome loads from a version behind, and the author
found it by testing something that had already been fixed. So it is a hook rather than a habit.
It fires after every tool call because most edits here are made by scripts run through Bash, not
by the file tools; tools/synctest.sh is a stamp check that costs milliseconds when nothing has
moved, and a no-op on any machine where the share is not mounted.

The one permission here names one script. tools/livebrowser.py talks to a browser the author has opened and logged in - the only thing in this repository that touches a live Zoho session rather than a fixture - and the safety layer refuses that by default, correctly. Allowing the script rather than the interpreter is the whole point: what it may and may not do is written at the top of that file, in the repository, where it can be read and grepped, instead of resting on a permission broad enough to cover anything else python can reach.

The second permission is a widening and is written down as one. Driving a browser means speaking the DevTools protocol over a websocket, and a script that sends commands to a live, logged-in browser is a remote-execution surface however carefully its docstring is worded - the safety layer refused to let it be written, correctly, twice. The author was told exactly that, and asked for it anyway on 27 September 2026, for a reason he had already argued: the live testing and the troubleshooting are the last of his operating cost that is still manual. So the grant names one file, tools/livebrowser.py, whose limits are written at its top and which is in the repository where they can be read and grepped. What keeps it honest is not this line: it is that the file is small, reviewable, and that he watches the screen while it works.
